source.title: Concept Steerers: Leveraging K-Sparse Autoencoders for Test-Time Controllable Generations

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The study uses k-sparse autoencoders to identify and steer concepts in diffusion-model text embeddings, but reports steering performance rather than testing superposition geometry, feature competition, or whether SAE features are complete or canonical units.
record.gate_note: The paper reports concept-steering outcomes, including unsafe-content rates. These show the performance of the proposed intervention; they do not test the listed versions’ claims about superposition, capacity pressure, LLM representations, feature completeness, or feature dimensionality. The reported steering results are recorded as findings about SAE-based concept control in diffusion models, not as tests of those versions.
record.test_reason: The study trains k-SAEs on diffusion text-encoder embeddings and uses them as a tool to steer concepts. It reports only steering performance (ASR, FID, CLIP, inference time) against other safety methods. It does not measure superposition geometry, capacity competition, polysemanticity causes, LLM feature distribution, SAE completeness or canonicity, or feature dimensionality. The k-SAE 'capacity' ablation (Table 4b) varies dictionary size for steering ASR only. The 'monosemantic' label is asserted, not measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that k-SAEs isolate 'monosemantic' concepts in text embeddings that enable test-time steering (unsafe-concept removal, styles, attributes). They report no retraining, preserved quality (user study near 50/50) and adversarial robustness. They add that the simpler linear steering variants fail, and that high λ can hurt object and identity consistency.
record.recipe_differences: Applies k-sparse autoencoders to text-encoder embeddings in text-to-image diffusion models and steers generations at test time; it does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported nudity-removal outcome varies with text-encoder layer, SAE expansion factor, and steering strength. Later layers performed better in the reported layer comparisons; expansion-factor differences were described as relatively minor; lower λ produced lower nudity ASR. The paper also reports layer-dependent violence ASR.

fits_no_version.finding: k-SAE latents trained on diffusion text-encoder embeddings enable test-time steering. Nudity ASR on I2P falls from 17.8 to 0.36; violence ASR falls from 99.6 to 43.7. Later layers steer better, and expansion factor matters little.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE-derived directions in text-to-image text encoders can act as steering vectors for concept removal or injection; this is performance evidence, not evidence about superposition.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the listed ASR results. The text notes that Ring-A-Bell and MMA-Diffusion are small datasets and that some performance gaps amount to only a few images. The reported measures concern concept-steering performance, not the representation claims in the listed versions.
record.rows_left_out: No results left out. Qualitative style and object-attribute examples are not separately tabulated as rows because they do not test any listed version.

untested.parts: No toy models, geometry or sparsity transition.
No capacity-competition analysis; the expansion-factor ablation reports only steering ASR.
No analysis of the causes of polysemantic neurons.
Diffusion text encoders (CLIP/T5), not LLMs. Feature interpretability is asserted via steering, not measured.
No test of completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features.
No comparison of one-dimensional and multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: Tool-use paper. Monosemanticity is claimed from steering success, not tested. Uncertainty is not reported, and some gaps amount to only 1–7 images. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network experiment or measurement of overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry.
No test of features competing for capacity, important features receiving dedicated dimensions, or other features sharing dimensions.
No test of alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
The study uses diffusion-model text encoders, not LLMs, and does not measure whether LLM activations are distributed across neurons or whether SAE features recover LLM representations.
No test of whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of a model’s representation.
No comparison of one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.
